scenes.narration: Subnetting scares a lot of people. But it's really just cutting up a block of addresses, like mailboxes in an apartment lobby. Let's cut one up together.

lines.t: But it's just cutting up mailboxes.

scenes.heading: The apartment mailboxes
scenes.narration: Imagine a lobby with two hundred and fifty-six mail slots. That's one network. The building manager gives each floor its own group of slots. That's subnetting. The size of each group is set by the subnet mask. The first slot is the name of the group, the network address. The last slot is the shout-to-everyone slot, the broadcast address. That leaves the slots in between for real residents, the usable hosts.

items.story: A group of slots for one floor

scenes.heading: The one formula
scenes.narration: There's one formula to remember. Count the host bits, which are the zeros in the mask. Two to the power of those bits gives you every address. Take away two, for the network and broadcast slots. The jump between subnets, called the block size, is two hundred and fifty-six minus the last mask number. So with one ninety-two, you jump in blocks of sixty-four.

lines.note: Count the zeros in the mask
Subnet IDs jump in blocks of 64

scenes.heading: Fixed size vs VLSM
scenes.narration: Now the clever part. Say three floors need ten, fifty and a hundred slots. With fixed-size groups, every floor gets the same size, so lots of slots are wasted. With V L S M, each floor gets a group that actually fits. Waste drops from a hundred and four slots down to forty-eight.

scenes.heading: Classic slip-ups
scenes.narration: Here are the classic slip-ups. People forget to subtract two, so a slash thirty has only two usable hosts, not four. They think a Class C network always uses slash twenty-four, but you can pick any mask. And with V L S M, always hand out the biggest groups first, so nothing overlaps.

items.right: Any mask can be used to subnet it

items.wrong: Hand out the smallest subnets first
items.right: VLSM: largest first, so nothing overlaps

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A subnet is one group of slots, sized by the mask. Usable hosts are two to the power of the host bits, minus two. And with V L S M, hand out the biggest groups first. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva subnetting lab.

points.t: A subnet is one group of slots, sized by the mask
VLSM: hand out the biggest groups first
